items.title: Posterior computation error budget
items.statement:
Fix a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ and a bounded measurable functional
$f:E\to\mathbb R$, with $\|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in E}|f(x)|<\infty$. All
target laws below are probability measures on this same space. If a model or
discretization originally uses another state space, specify its measurable
embedding into $E$ and compare its pushforward law; no identification of
different state spaces is implicit. A **posterior law** here is the probability
law for the unknown at the specified computation stage, conditional on the same
fixed observed data. For a probability law $\mu$, write
$\mu(f):=\int_E f\,d\mu$.

Name the successive posterior laws as follows: $\mu_\star$ is the intended
target; $\mu_{\rm model}$ is the posterior under the selected statistical or
physical model; $\mu_{\rm solver}$ is the posterior after replacing the exact
forward or PDE solution by the declared numerical solver output; and
$\mu_{\rm disc}$ is the posterior after the declared finite-dimensional
discretization. These labels refer to the exact adjacent laws recorded for the
computation, even when two stages happen to agree.

Let $K$ be the implemented probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$. An
**invariant law** $\pi_K$ for $K$ is a probability measure satisfying
$$\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi_K(dx)=\pi_K(A)\qquad(A\in\mathcal E).$$
Choose and report which invariant law is used if $K$ has more than one. If no
invariant law has been established, the invariant-kernel and burn-in terms
below are unavailable; they are not set to zero. Let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a
time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative to its
natural filtration, with initial probability law $\lambda$. For burn-in length
$b\ge0$ and retained sample size $N\ge1$, set
$$\bar f_{b,N}:=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N f(X_{b+j}),$$
and let $\mathbb E_\lambda$ denote expectation under this initial law and the
chain's transition randomness.

When all stages are present, define the component errors
$$\begin{aligned}\delta_{\rm model}&:=|\mu_\star(f)-\mu_{\rm model}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm solver}&:=|\mu_{\rm model}(f)-\mu_{\rm solver}(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm disc}&:=|\mu_{\rm solver}(f)-\mu_{\rm disc}(f)|,\\ \delta_K&:=|\mu_{\rm disc}(f)-\pi_K(f)|,\\ \delta_{\rm burn}&:=|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|,\\ \delta_{\rm MC}&:=|\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}-\bar f_{b,N}|.\end{aligned}$$
The last component is random and the earlier components are fixed for the
declared data and computation. The **posterior computation error budget** is
$$\mathcal B_f:=\delta_{\rm model}+\delta_{\rm solver}+\delta_{\rm disc}+\delta_K+\delta_{\rm burn}+\delta_{\rm MC}.$$
If a computation stops before one of these stages, report the shorter reference
chain and its component terms. The term $\delta_K$ measures the invariant-law
discrepancy induced by the implemented transition rule; it is not a one-step
distance between kernels. A one-step kernel error cannot replace it without a
separate perturbation theorem with its own hypotheses.

The successive scalar references are arranged as this directed error chain;
each arrow is labelled by the absolute difference of its endpoints.

```tikzcd
\mu_\star(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm model}"] &
\mu_{\rm model}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm solver}"] &
\mu_{\rm solver}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm disc}"] &
\mu_{\rm disc}(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_K"] &
\pi_K(f) \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm burn}"] &
\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N} \arrow[r, "\delta_{\rm MC}"] &
\bar f_{b,N}
```

The budget is a bookkeeping bound only when its components are supplied with
estimators or verified bounds; an unavailable component is reported as
unquantified rather than silently set to zero. In particular, invariance alone
does not provide a burn-in estimate, a mixing rate, or a Monte Carlo error
estimate.

references.locator: §4.2, Assumptions 4.7 and Theorems 4.8–4.9 (PDF pp. 40–43): posterior changes caused by a potential approximation and the hypotheses needed for a Hellinger rate.

references.title: S. L. Cotter, G. O. Roberts, A. M. Stuart, and D. White, MCMC Methods for Functions: Modifying Old Algorithms to Make Them Faster
references.locator: §4.2, pCN proposal (4.7)–(4.11), and §6.1, Theorem 6.2: exact invariant-kernel context for function-space posterior computation.

references.title: Charles J. Geyer, Markov Chain Monte Carlo Lecture Notes
references.locator: §1.6.2, equation (1.9) and the following caution (printed pp. 8–11; PDF pp. 12–15): stationary-chain variance of a sample mean and limits on CLT conclusions.

items.axiom_use: The reference-chain bookkeeping is choice-free. AC is assumed only through the library's time-homogeneous Markov-chain interface, which supplies conditional-probability classes; the definition makes no chain-existence assertion and selects no sample paths.

items.title: Bounded posterior functionals and stationary sample error
items.statement:
Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be a measurable space, let $\mu,\nu$ be probability
measures on it, and let $f:E\to\mathbb R$ be measurable with
$|f|\le M$ for some $0\le M<\infty$. Use the library convention
$$\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}:=\sup_{A\in\mathcal E}|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|.$$
Then
$$|\mu(f)-\nu(f)|\le2M\|\mu-\nu\|_{\rm TV}.$$

For the complete posterior computation error budget defined above, the
pathwise total error satisfies
$$|\mu_\star(f)-\bar f_{b,N}|\le\mathcal B_f.$$
This is a telescoping bound; it does not estimate any component.

Separately, let $(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with transition kernel $K$, invariant law $\pi_K$, and initial law
$X_0\sim\pi_K$, and use the same bounded functional $f$. Put
$$\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}(f(X_0),f(X_k))\qquad(k\ge0).$$
If $\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\gamma_k|<\infty$, then for every burn-in $b\ge0$ and
sample size $N\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\left[|\bar f_{b,N}-\pi_K(f)|^2\right]=\frac{1}{N^2}\left[N\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{N-1}(N-k)\gamma_k\right]\le\frac{\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty|\gamma_k|}{N}.$$
The sample bound assumes stationarity; for a nonstationary start, the budget
keeps $|\pi_K(f)-\mathbb E_\lambda\bar f_{b,N}|$ as a separate burn-in term.
This finite-$N$ variance bound is not a central limit theorem or a confidence
interval.

references.title: Alison L. Gibbs and Francis Edward Su, On Choosing and Bounding Probability Metrics, International Statistical Review 70(3) (2002)
references.locator: §2, total-variation definition and bounded-function dual form (equation (2)); §5 discussion of bounded expected-loss error.

references.title: David A. Levin, Yuval Peres, and Elizabeth L. Wilmer, Markov Chains and Mixing Times, second edition
references.locator: §4.1, Proposition 4.5 and full proof (PDF pp. 48–49): finite-state bounded-function dual form and total-variation normalization.

references.title: Charles J. Geyer, Markov Chain Monte Carlo Lecture Notes
references.locator: §1.6.2, equation (1.9) and the following caution (printed pp. 8–11; PDF pp. 12–15): exact stationary sample-mean variance and limits on CLT conclusions.

title: Posterior computation and error accounting — Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: An exact invariant kernel can be biased over a short run
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $E=\{-1,+1\}$ with the discrete sigma-algebra $2^E$, and let
the target posterior $\pi$ assign mass $1/2$ to each state. For
$0<\varepsilon<1/2$, define
$$K_\varepsilon(x,A):=(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf1_A(x)+\varepsilon\mathbf1_A(-x)\qquad(x\in E,\ A\subseteq E).$$
Take $\varepsilon=1/1000$. The Ionescu--Tulcea construction supplies a
time-homogeneous Markov chain on canonical path space with initial law
$\delta_{+1}$ and transition kernel $K_\varepsilon$. Use this chain with its
natural filtration, retain the next $N=100$ draws, and set the bounded
functional $f(x)=x$. The target law $\pi$ is
invariant for this exact kernel, but the expected reported average is
$$\mathbb E\left[\frac1{100}\sum_{j=1}^{100}X_j\right]=\frac{499}{100}\left(1-\left(\frac{499}{500}\right)^{100}\right)>0=\pi(f).$$
For the error ledger take each deterministic posterior stage to be $\pi$;
then the invariant-kernel error is zero while the finite-run burn-in error is
positive.

references.title: David A. Levin, Yuval Peres, and Elizabeth L. Wilmer, Markov Chains and Mixing Times, second edition
references.locator: §4.1, Example 4.1 and the total-variation discussion of the two-state chain.

items.axiom_use: AC is used through conditional-expectation existence for the time-homogeneous chain interface and through the Ionescu--Tulcea construction. Invariance and the finite-state calculations use no additional choice.

items.title: Correct invariance can coexist with low effective sample size
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $E=\{-1,+1\}$ with the discrete sigma-algebra $2^E$, and let
the target posterior $\pi$ be uniform on $E$. For $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, define
$$K_\varepsilon(x,A):=(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf1_A(x)+\varepsilon\mathbf1_A(-x)\qquad(x\in E,\ A\subseteq E),$$
and set $\varepsilon=1/100$. The Ionescu--Tulcea construction supplies a
time-homogeneous Markov chain on canonical path space with initial law $\pi$
and transition kernel $K_\varepsilon$. Use this chain with its natural
filtration and set $f(x)=x$. Define its lag-$k$ autocorrelation by
$$\rho_f(k):=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(f(X_0),f(X_k))}{\operatorname{Var}(f(X_0))}.$$
For every $k\ge1$, $\rho_f(k)=(49/50)^k$. Its integrated autocorrelation
time $\tau_f:=1+2\sum_{k=1}^\infty\rho_f(k)$ is therefore $99$, so the
theoretical functional-specific effective sample size of $N=10{,}000$ draws is
$$\operatorname{ESS}_f(10{,}000)=\frac{10{,}000}{99}\approx101.01.$$
The invariant law is exactly the target posterior, while this functional has
only about one percent of the nominal independent-sample size. This is the
theoretical ESS from the stationary autocorrelation sequence, not an empirical
finite-run ESS estimate, and it asserts no central limit theorem.

references.title: Aki Vehtari et al., Rank-normalization, folding, and localization: An improved R-hat for assessing convergence of MCMC
references.locator: §3.2, equations (7)–(9) and the discussion that ESS is functional-specific and is not a substitute for MCSE.

items.axiom_use: AC is used through conditional-expectation existence for the Markov-chain interface and invariant-initial-law theorem, and through the Ionescu--Tulcea construction. The finite transition, covariance, and geometric-series calculations use no additional choice and establish no central limit theorem.

items.title: A biased forward solve shifts a Gaussian posterior
items.statement:
Let the scalar parameter $u$ have prior density
$$p_0(u)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2},$$
and observe $y=0$ with unit-variance Gaussian noise. The exact forward map is
$G(u)=u$, while a deliberately biased numerical forward/PDE solver reports
$\widetilde G(u)=u+2$. At $y=0$, use likelihoods
$L(u)=\exp(-G(u)^2/2)$ and
$\widetilde L(u)=\exp(-\widetilde G(u)^2/2)$; the common Gaussian density
constant cancels when normalizing. Define each fixed-data posterior by
normalizing the prior times its stated likelihood. The exact posterior is
$N(0,1/2)$ and the solver posterior is $N(-1,1/2)$. For the bounded functional
$f(u)=\mathbf 1_{(-\infty,0]}(u)$, their expectations are respectively
$$\Pi(f)=\tfrac12,\qquad \widetilde\Pi(f)=\Phi_0(\sqrt2)>\tfrac12,$$
where
$$\Phi_0(t):=\int_{-\infty}^{t}(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}\,dz.$$
The discrepancy is in the forward-solver stage of the posterior error budget;
this toy solver assumption makes no claim about the bias of any general PDE
discretization.
items.axiom_use: AC is assumed by the library normal-law interface. Once the prior and likelihood densities are specified, the completion-of-square and expectation calculations are choice-free.
